cards.text: Here's a short one, friend: Psalm 125, a song of ascents. It's about people who trust in the LORD. And it opens with one BIG picture.

cards.question: The psalm says those who trust in the LORD are like a mountain. Which one?

cards.text: Mount Zion. A MOUNTAIN, friend. Meanwhile I spent years in a junk drawer getting shoved to the back every time somebody needed tape.

cards.question: What does the psalm say about Mount Zion that makes it a picture of people who trust the LORD?
The psalm says Mount Zion lasts only for a season.

cards.text: Then the picture gets bigger. Jerusalem sits with mountains all around it, like a city with its own bodyguards made of ROCK.

cards.question: The mountains surround Jerusalem. In the same way, who surrounds the LORD's people?
How long does the psalm say the LORD surrounds His people?

cards.text: Now the wicked show up, scepter and all. And there's land allotted to the righteous sitting right there.

cards.question: The psalm says the scepter of the wicked will rest on the land allotted to the righteous.

cards.text: The psalm even gives a reason, and it's about what happens to the righteous. I bet you've seen it at work: one crooked boss in charge, and pretty soon the WHOLE office is cutting corners.

cards.question: Why won't the scepter of the wicked rest on the land allotted to the righteous?

answers.text: So the righteous won't turn to injustice
So the righteous can grow their harvest
So the wicked will turn and repent

cards.text: Then the song turns into a prayer, aimed straight at the LORD. It's about people who are good and upright in heart.

cards.question: What does the psalm ask the LORD to do for those who are good and upright in heart?

cards.text: Then the flip side. Not everybody stays upright. Some people make a turn, and it's not the scenic route.

cards.question: Those who turn to ___ ways, the LORD will banish with the evildoers.

cards.text: And the very last line is a blessing: "Peace be upon Israel." Five verses, friend, and that little song stands like a MOUNTAIN.

findings.problem: The card asks the baker to guess which mountain the line names (Zion, Sinai or Carmel). Nothing on card 1 lets the baker reason it out. It guesses a word of the line, like the bad Psalm 23 example 'oil, myrrh or perfume?', and is a pure-luck pick.

rule.text: Never ask the baker to guess the next words of a line.

findings.problem: The story card tells nothing new from the passage. It repeats the Mount Zion answer from card 2 and adds a joke. It works as a recap card, with the joke not riding on a new piece of the passage. Its 'shoved to the back' contrast also leans the baker toward card 4's answer, 'It cannot be moved'.

The right answer 'Both now and forevermore' is the verse's exact wording and sounds far more like the Bible than the wrong answers 'Until the danger passes' and 'Only during the feasts', so it stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: 'Now the wicked show up, scepter and all' presents the wicked arriving as an event. Psalm 125:3 only says the scepter of the wicked will not rest on the land allotted to the righteous. It never says the wicked show up, and the text doesn't clearly imply it.

rule.text: Retelling: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: The setup says the reason is 'about what happens to the righteous'. That rules out card 12's wrong answer 'So the wicked will turn and repent'. The office joke (a crooked boss leading everyone to cut corners) then gives away card 12's answer outright.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The joke uses the word 'crooked' ('one crooked boss in charge'). That is the right answer to card 16's fill in the blank ('Those who turn to ___ ways'), so the later answer is given away.

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The humor is mild throughout. Cards 1, 9, 13 and 15 read like a pleasant dad narrating, and the jokes on cards 6 and 17 are light. Nothing reaches the laugh-out-loud level the voice calls for, even though the passage has room for real laughs that don't muddy facts.

rule.text: If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
